source.title: Structure-Specific Representational Priors Causally Control the Grokking Delay

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests delayed generalization and representation timing on modular addition, but uses structure-injection and probing interventions rather than reproducing the original method.
record.gate_note: Rows cover the paper's own modular-addition outcomes and representation-timing measurements. Cited results from prior work are not included. The paper does not sweep training-set size, test natural data or large models, or identify whether networks converge to the same full algorithm across runs.
record.test_reason: The plain baseline (Nanda-style one-layer transformer, p=97, 30% split, AdamW wd 1.0) shows the grokking delay (V1). Representation probes across all 95 runs show embedding Fourier concentration and class clustering moving before the accuracy jump (V2). Most other results are interventions that inject structure or control the norm. Those bear on what controls the delay, not on any listed version as stated.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. More precisely, the authors conclude three things in this modular-addition setting. First, the grokking delay is causally the time to form the right representational structure, with 'right' decided at the feature level: true structure accelerates, coherent sibling structure preserves, random structure abolishes. Second, the effect is not mediated by weight norm (the norm-matched control gives 0/15). Third, removing the prior's norm side-effect turns it into a reliable accelerator; the norm-clamp gives a median 8.6×.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a one-layer modular-addition transformer but adds supervised-contrastive structure-injection conditions, norm-matched controls, and representation probes rather than reproducing the original training recipe. Also tests norm-control variants and Grokfast composition.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome depends on the positive-set structure and contrastive strength. True structure's acceleration is seed- and dose-dependent; norm-clamp, norm-replay, adaptive control, and annealing differ in speed. Grokfast composition changes sharply with λgf.

fits_no_version.finding: Under identical loss form and strength, a true-structure contrastive prior generalizes in 22/30 runs and can accelerate grokking (best 2.75×). A wrong-but-coherent (a−b) prior generalizes in 14/15 without median acceleration. A random-partition prior generalizes in 0/20.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The grokking delay is causally the time to form task-compatible representational structure; feature-family compatibility sets whether generalization occurs, and true structure sets its speed.

fits_no_version.finding: Replaying the inflated SupCon norm trajectory onto plain cross-entropy training yields 0/15 generalization, with logit-scale saturation. Holding the norm low while keeping the prior speeds grokking monotonically (clamp at 45: 8.6×; replay 6.6×; adaptive 2.8×; anneal 1.7×).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Weight norm controls the grokking timescale via logit saturation under structure-agnostic training, but a structural prior can generalize at norms where plain cross-entropy cannot.

fits_no_version.finding: Grokfast accelerates baseline grokking (5/5; ratios 0.43–0.85) but stalls the structural prior at default strength (0/10), and gives 5/10 when de-tuned.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimizer-side and representation-side grokking accelerators do not beneficially compose.

record.problems: Evidence is limited to one algorithmic task and one small architecture, with typically 5–10 runs per condition and a 50,000-epoch censoring budget. The paper states transfer to larger models and natural data is untested. Some representation results are presented in figures without numeric values, and training-set size is not varied.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant own results left out.

untested.parts: Dependence of the delay on training-set size (only a 30% split is used).
Full Fourier-circuit identification and the later removal (clean-up) of memorizing components.
All: no non-algorithmic data and no initialization-scale/lazy-rich sweep.
All: no LLM pretraining or fine-tuning.
Efficiency comparison of circuits, critical dataset size, ungrokking. The norm manipulations are not framed or measured as efficiency.
All: algorithms are not compared across runs.
All: no optimizer-instability or floating-point controls.

missing.what: Baseline tfit and delay (tgen−tfit) values per seed or median
Baseline-condition lead time between Fourier or cluster-probe rise and the accuracy jump
Pooled stall reduction for the mitigations: 0/40 vs 6/20, p=7.7×10^-4

record.verdict_notes: Most rows are interventions (structure injection, norm control, accelerators) and the study's own accelerator performance. I unlinked them from V1: they show the delay can be manipulated, not whether V1 holds in the standard setting. The random-partition and norm-matched failures are induced, so they do not challenge V1. V2 support rests on embedding-level progress measures with a lenient 'precedes' threshold; memorization clean-up is not measured. Single author, preprint; it cites a concurrent companion paper for some results, which are not counted here.

versions.untested_parts: Training-set-size dependence is untested: the study uses a 30% training split and does not vary dataset size. The study reports test-accuracy thresholds and training-fit criteria, but does not tabulate exact train-accuracy and chance-level test-accuracy values over time for each run.
The study probes representation formation and its timing, but does not directly identify the full Fourier multiplication circuit or measure later removal of memorizing components.
No non-algorithmic data or initialization-scale/lazy-to-rich sweep.
No LLM pretraining or fine-tuning on realistic data.

The study tests norm-related controls and their effects on grokking, but does not test whether low norm favors a more efficient generalizing circuit or whether a critical dataset size and ungrokking follow.
The study does not identify and compare the algorithms learned across runs.
No controlled test of adaptive-optimizer instabilities or floating-point limits in the softmax.

rows.subject: one-layer decoder-only transformer (aggregate runs)
rows.operation_detail: Track held-out representation class cosine gap during training
rows.measure: Timing of class-cluster formation relative to test-accuracy generalization
rows.value: Across all 95 runs, none generalizes before its representation probes move; true-structure class cosine gap rises during the plateau, thousands of epochs before the accuracy jump.
rows.note: The text operationalizes an earlier crossing of cosine gap >0.05 or Fourier top-8 fraction >0.45 for every run that reaches 95% test accuracy.
rows.check: The 'precedes' criterion is a weak threshold (cosine gap >0.05 or Fourier top-8 >0.45 crossed earlier). Lead times are shown only in Fig. 2 medians. The 'thousands of epochs' statement refers to SupCon-true runs, not the baseline.

rows.note: The paper reports that shuffled training shows no task-structure formation and the norm-matched control forms no structure.
rows.check: Fourier concentration is an embedding-level progress measure, not identification of the full circuit. Removal of memorizing components is not measured.

source_check.notes: The precedence criterion uses either probe threshold and is non-vacuous in 51 generalizing runs; the remaining runs satisfy it trivially. Figure 2 shows medians, so it does not establish numerical lead times for individual runs.

Full circuit identification and memorization-component removal not measured.
statements.problem: The representation-timing claim is supported, but the no-code description conflicts with Appendix A, Table 3.
